title: Radical reactions
goal: Follow single electrons with fish-hook arrows: how radical chains start, carry on and choose where to react.

problemSets.title: Radical chains
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A radical breaks a weak bond and makes a new radical, so one initiation event drives a long chain.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A **radical** has an unpaired electron. Radical steps move electrons *one at a time*, drawn with **fish-hook arrows** (half arrowheads). Making a bond between a radical and a molecule takes three fish-hooks: one from the radical, and one from each electron of the bond that breaks.

A radical reaction is a **chain**:

- **initiation** makes the first radicals, often by breaking a weak bond (Br–Br with light, or the O–O of a peroxide on heating)
- **propagation** steps each use up one radical and make another, so the chain carries on
- **termination**, when two radicals meet, ends a chain; it is rare, because radicals are so dilute

Radicals are more stable when more substituted (tertiary > secondary > primary) and when delocalised, as next to a C=C. The weakest C–H bond is the one whose radical is most stable.

setItems.whyThisOne: The two propagation steps of every halogenation: take H, then take Br.
The allylic C–H is the weakest: its radical is shared over both ends of the allyl unit.
With a peroxide, Br adds first, so it ends on the carbon a cation route would not choose.

problemSets.title: Selectivity
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Bromine is choosy and chlorine is not, because their H-abstraction steps have late and early transition states.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Propane has six **primary** hydrogens and two **secondary** ones. The secondary C–H bond is weaker, because it gives the more stable secondary radical. How much that matters depends on the halogen:

- **Cl•** forms a strong H–Cl bond, so taking any hydrogen is *exothermic*. The transition state comes **early**, looks like the starting materials and hardly feels which radical will form: about 55% 2-chloropropane, 45% 1-chloropropane
- **Br•** forms a weaker H–Br bond, so the step is *endothermic*. The transition state comes **late**, looks like the radical, and feels its stability fully: about 97% 2-bromopropane

This is the **Hammond postulate**: a transition state resembles whichever side of the step is closer to it in energy. The more reactive reagent is the less selective one.

setItems.whyThisOne: Chlorine takes both kinds of hydrogen: two products in similar amounts.
Bromine takes almost only the secondary hydrogen: the same reaction, a very different outcome.

problemSets.title: Tin hydride chemistry
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Bu₃Sn• pulls off Br or attacks C=S, and Bu₃SnH hands back a hydrogen: a chain that makes C–H bonds and rings.
problemSets.conceptCard:
**Tributyltin hydride**, Bu₃SnH, has a weak Sn–H bond. A little **AIBN** starts the chain: on heating it loses N₂ to give carbon radicals, which take H from tin and make the tin radical, **Bu₃Sn•**.

The chain then has two propagation steps:

1. Bu₃Sn• removes an atom from the substrate: a halogen (strong Sn–Br) or the sulfur of a C=S (strong Sn–S), and a carbon radical is left
2. the carbon radical takes H from Bu₃SnH and gives back Bu₃Sn•

In between, the carbon radical can do something useful. In the **Barton–McCombie** deoxygenation it fragments (*β-scission*) to make a strong C=O. In a **radical cyclisation** it adds to an alkene in its own chain; a five-membered ring forms fastest (**5-exo-trig**), with its new radical outside the ring.

Tin compounds are toxic, so newer methods use silanes such as (Me₃Si)₃SiH in the same way.

setItems.whyThisOne: Where the tin radical comes from: AIBN loses N₂, then takes H from tin.
An alcohol becomes an alkane: tin adds to C=S and a C=O forms as the C–O bond breaks.
A radical closes a ring onto its own alkene: five-membered beats six-membered.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Which bond breaks, where does each single electron go, and which radical forms?
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: Which end of the alkene does the radical bond to?
Which bond does the radical break?
